title: AP Physics C: Mechanics - Energy and momentum

skills.name: Choose the principle that fits the question: energy, work and friction, momentum or impulse
Find a force from Newton's laws: balanced forces, F = ma, friction = μN
Work by a constant force, W = Fd cos θ, including its sign
Work by a changing force, W = ∫F dx
Net work equals the change in kinetic energy, ΔK = ΣW
Potential energy of gravity near Earth (mgΔy) and of a spring (½kx²)
Force from potential energy, F = −dU/dx, and equilibrium on a U(x) curve
Conservation of mechanical energy: K + U stays the same with no friction
Energy with friction: work by friction changes K + U
Gravitational potential energy far from Earth, U = −GMm/r, and escape speed
Power: P = ΔE/Δt on average, P = Fv at an instant
Momentum p = mv and impulse J = ∫F dt = Δp
Center of mass of a system, and its velocity
Conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions, in 1D and 2D
Elastic or inelastic: is kinetic energy kept in a collision?
Split a problem into stages: a collision (momentum) then a motion (energy)

problems.title: Pushing a cart
problems.prompt: A {m} kg {thing} starts at rest on a frictionless {track}. You push it with a constant {F} N horizontal force for {d} m.

steps.prompt: Which principle links your push to the {thing}'s final speed, using the force and the distance but not the time?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved here: your push does work on the {thing} and adds energy.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved here: your push is an outside force.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: You'd first need the time from kinematics. Work-energy uses the force and the distance directly.

steps.hint: You know a force and a distance. Force times distance is work, and the net work on the {thing} changes its kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: How much work does your push do on the {thing}, in joules?
steps.hint: The force points along the motion, so W = Fd = {F} × {d}.

steps.prompt: Derive an expression for the {thing}'s final speed, in terms of F, d and m.
steps.hint: All the work becomes kinetic energy: ½mv² = Fd. Solve for v.

steps.prompt: What is the {thing}'s final speed, in m/s?
If the {thing} had twice the mass, with the same push over the same distance, how would its final speed change?
options: It would be 1/√2 ≈ 0.71 times as large
It would be half as large
It would be the same
It would be twice as large
steps.answer: It would be 1/√2 ≈ 0.71 times as large

feedback.It would be half as large: The work Fd is the same, so ½mv² is the same: doubling m divides v² by 2, so v is divided by √2, not 2.
feedback.It would be the same: The push does the same work, but the same kinetic energy in twice the mass means a lower speed.
feedback.It would be twice as large: A heavier {thing} speeds up less: the same work goes into twice the mass.

steps.hint: From your formula, v = √(2Fd/m). What happens to v when m is doubled?

problems.title: A push shown on a graph
problems.prompt: A {m} kg {thing} starts at rest on a frictionless {track}. A horizontal force acts on it along the x-axis. The graph shows the force F against the position x, from x = 0 to x = {c} m. A negative F points backward.

steps.prompt: Which principle links the force on the graph to the {thing}'s speed at x = {c} m?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the push is an outside force that adds energy.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the push is an outside force on the {thing}.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs force against time, and this graph gives force against position.

steps.hint: The graph gives force against position. A force over a distance does work, and net work changes kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: How do you find the work the force does from x = 0 to x = {c} m?
options: The area between the F–x graph and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = {c} m, counting area below the axis as negative
The slope of the F–x graph
The largest force times {c} m
steps.answer: The area between the F–x graph and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = {c} m, counting area below the axis as negative

feedback.The slope of the F–x graph: The slope says how fast the force changes with position, not how much work it does.
feedback.The largest force times {c} m: That treats the force as {F0} N the whole way, but it starts at 0, drops back to 0 and then points backward.

steps.hint: Work is ∫F dx, which is the area between the graph and the x-axis.

steps.prompt: How much work does the force do from x = 0 to x = {a} m, in joules?
steps.hint: That part of the graph is a triangle: area = ½ × {a} m × {F0} N.

steps.prompt: How much work does the force do from x = 0 to x = {c} m, in joules?
steps.hint: Add the areas above the axis (a triangle, a rectangle and a triangle) and subtract the small triangle below the axis, ½ × {q} × {F1}.

steps.prompt: What is the {thing}'s speed at x = {c} m, in m/s?
steps.hint: All {W:.2f} J of net work becomes kinetic energy: ½({m})v² = {W:.2f}.

steps.prompt: Where between x = 0 and x = {c} m is the {thing} moving fastest?
options: At x = {z} m, where the force drops to zero
At x = {c} m, at the end of the push
At x = {a} m, where the force first reaches its largest value
Anywhere from x = {a} m to x = {b} m, because the force is constant there
steps.answer: At x = {z} m, where the force drops to zero

feedback.At x = {c} m, at the end of the push: After x = {z} m the force points backward, so it does negative work and the {thing} slows down.
feedback.At x = {a} m, where the force first reac: The largest force means the largest acceleration, not the largest speed. The {thing} keeps speeding up after that.
feedback.Anywhere from x = {a} m to x = {b} m, be: A constant forward force means constant acceleration, so the speed keeps growing there.

steps.hint: Ask, at each part of the graph: is the force speeding the {thing} up or slowing it down?

problems.title: Pulling at an angle
problems.prompt: A {m} kg {thing} starts at rest on a level {surface}. A rope pulls it {d} m with a constant {F} N force at θ = {theta}° above the horizontal, and the {thing} slides. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the {thing} and the {surface} is μ = {mu:.2f}. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.prompt: Which principle links the rope's pull, friction and the {d} m to the {thing}'s final speed?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the rope adds energy and friction turns some into heat.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the rope and friction are outside forces on the {thing}.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs how long the forces act, and you know the distance, not the time.

steps.hint: Forces acting over a distance do work. Add up every force's work, and the total changes the {thing}'s kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: Derive an expression for the normal force on the {thing}, in terms of m, g, F and θ.
steps.hint: Nothing moves up or down, so the vertical forces balance: N + F sin θ = mg. The rope lifts part of the weight.

steps.prompt: How much work does the rope do on the {thing}, in joules?
steps.hint: Only the part of the pull along the motion does work: W = Fd cos θ = {F} × {d} × cos {theta}°.

steps.prompt: How much work do gravity and the normal force do on the {thing}?
options: None, because each force is perpendicular to the motion
Gravity does negative work, because it pulls down on the {thing}
The normal force does positive work, because it pushes up on the {thing}
Each does work, but the two amounts cancel
steps.answer: None, because each force is perpendicular to the motion

feedback.Gravity does negative work, because it p: Work needs a force along the motion. The {thing} moves sideways and gravity points straight down, so cos 90° = 0.
feedback.The normal force does positive work, bec: The normal force points straight up and the {thing} moves sideways, so it does no work.
feedback.Each does work, but the two amounts canc: Neither does any work at all: both are perpendicular to the motion, so W = Fd cos 90° = 0 for each.

steps.hint: W = Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the motion.

steps.prompt: Suppose the rope pulled horizontally with the same {F} N force instead. How would the size of the work done by friction change?
options: It would be larger, because the normal force would grow to mg
It would be smaller, because a horizontal pull moves the {thing} more easily
It would be the same, because friction depends only on μ and the distance
steps.answer: It would be larger, because the normal force would grow to mg

feedback.It would be smaller, because a horizonta: Friction's size is μN, and it does not depend on how easily the {thing} moves. A horizontal rope no longer lifts, so N goes up.
feedback.It would be the same, because friction d: Friction is μN, and N depends on the rope: pulling upward at an angle lifts part of the weight and lowers N.

steps.hint: Friction's size is μN. Write N for the angled rope and for a horizontal rope, then compare.

steps.prompt: How much work does friction do on the {thing}, in joules? Include the sign.
steps.hint: W = −μNd, with N = mg − F sin θ = {N:.1f} N.

steps.prompt: Derive an expression for the {thing}'s speed after it moves a distance d, in terms of F, θ, μ, m, g and d.
steps.hint: Net work = Fd cos θ − μ(mg − F sin θ)d, and it all becomes kinetic energy: ½mv² = net work.

steps.prompt: What is the {thing}'s speed after {d} m, in m/s?
steps.hint: Net work = {Wrope:.0f} J + ({Wfric:.0f} J). Set ½({m})v² equal to it.

problems.title: A force that grows with distance
problems.prompt: A {m} kg block starts at rest on a frictionless surface. A force F(x) = αx², with α = {alpha} N/m², pushes it along the x-axis from x = 0 to x = D = {D} m.

steps.prompt: Which principle links the force F(x) over the distance D to the block's speed at x = D?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the force is an outside push that adds energy to the block.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the force is an outside push on the block.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the force as a function of time, and here it is given as a function of position.

steps.hint: The force is given along the path (as a function of x). A force over a distance does work, and net work changes kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: How do you find the work done by this force?
options: Integrate F(x) dx from x = 0 to x = D
Multiply the force at x = D by D
Multiply the average of F(0) and F(D) by D
steps.answer: Integrate F(x) dx from x = 0 to x = D

feedback.Multiply the force at x = D by D: That works only for a constant force, and this force changes with x.
feedback.Multiply the average of F(0) and F(D) by: Averaging the two ends works only for a force that grows in a straight line, and αx² curves.

steps.hint: The force changes as the block moves, so add up F dx over every small bit of the path.

steps.prompt: Derive an expression for the work done by the force from x = 0 to x = D, in terms of α and D.
steps.hint: ∫αx² dx = αx³/3. Evaluate it from 0 to D.

steps.prompt: How much work does the force do, in joules?
steps.hint: W = αD³/3 = {alpha} × {D}³ / 3.

steps.prompt: Derive an expression for the block's speed at x = D, in terms of α, D and m.
steps.hint: All the work becomes kinetic energy: ½mv² = αD³/3. Solve for v.

steps.prompt: What is the block's speed at x = D = {D} m, in m/s?
If the force pushed the block twice as far (to x = 2D), how would the block's final speed change?
options: It would be about 2.8 times as large (2√2)
It would be 2 times as large
It would be 4 times as large
It would be 8 times as large
steps.answer: It would be about 2.8 times as large (2√2)

feedback.It would be 2 times as large: The work is not proportional to D: it grows as D³, and the speed as the square root of that.
feedback.It would be 4 times as large: 4 would fit a speed proportional to D², but v grows as √(D³) = D^1.5.
feedback.It would be 8 times as large: 8 times is how the work grows (D³). The speed grows as the square root of the work: √8 ≈ 2.8.

steps.hint: v is proportional to √(D³) = D^1.5. Doubling D multiplies v by 2^1.5.

problems.title: Spring launches a block up a ramp
problems.prompt: A spring with k = 500 N/m is squeezed 0.15 m and launches a 0.20 kg block along a frictionless level track, which then curves up a frictionless ramp. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.prompt: Which principle links the squeezed spring to how high the block climbs, without working out any force's work?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: The work-energy theorem needs the spring's and gravity's work along the way, which the question asks you to avoid; with no friction, K + U stays the same.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the spring and gravity are outside forces on the block, which ends up stopped at the top.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the forces and how long they act, which you don't know, and it gives momentum, not height.

steps.hint: With no friction, only the spring and gravity do work, and both store energy. So the total of kinetic and potential energy stays the same.

steps.prompt: Put the forms of energy in the order the block has them, starting from the squeezed spring.
answer: Kinetic energy on the level track
Gravitational potential energy at the highest point on the ramp
steps.hint: The spring pushes the block (spring energy becomes motion), then the block slows as it climbs (motion becomes height).

steps.prompt: How much energy, in joules, is stored in the squeezed spring?
What is the block's speed on the level track, in m/s?
steps.hint: All the spring energy becomes kinetic energy: ½(0.20)v² = 5.625.

steps.prompt: How high up the ramp does the block rise, in meters?
steps.hint: All the energy becomes gravitational potential energy: mgh = 5.625, so h = 5.625 / (0.20 × 9.8).

steps.prompt: If the spring were squeezed twice as far (0.30 m), how would the height change?
options: 4 times as high
2 times as high
The same height

feedback.2 times as high: Spring energy is ½kx², so twice the squeeze stores 4 times the energy, not 2.
feedback.The same height: A bigger squeeze stores more energy, so the block climbs higher.

steps.hint: Spring energy is ½kx². Doubling x makes x² four times bigger, and the height follows the energy.

problems.title: Pendulum released from 37°
problems.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball hangs on a 1.2 m string. It is pulled aside until the string makes 37° with the vertical (cos 37° ≈ 0.80), then released from rest. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.prompt: Which principle gives the ball's speed at the bottom from its release height, without working out any force's work?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: The work-energy theorem needs each force's work along the swing, which the question asks you to avoid; the string does no work, so K + U stays the same.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: gravity and the string both pull on the ball, so its momentum keeps changing.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the forces and how long the swing takes, which you don't know.

steps.hint: The string always pulls at right angles to the ball's motion, so it does no work. Only gravity does work, and gravity's work is already counted as potential energy.

steps.prompt: How far, in meters, does the ball drop from its release point to the bottom of the swing?
steps.hint: The drop is L − L cos 37° = 1.2(1 − 0.80). Note L cos 37° is the height of the ball below the pivot, not the drop.

steps.prompt: What is the ball's speed at the bottom, in m/s?

problems.title: Block sliding down a rough ramp
problems.prompt: A 4.0 kg block starts at rest and slides 5.0 m down a ramp tilted 30° above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.prompt: Which principle links the block's start at rest to its speed at the bottom, with friction taking energy away?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: friction turns some of it into heat.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: gravity, the ramp and friction are outside forces on the block.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs how long the slide takes, which you don't know.

steps.hint: Friction does negative work, so K + U is not kept. Add the work of every force (gravity and friction) to get the change in kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: How far, in meters, does the block drop vertically?
steps.hint: The vertical drop is the distance along the ramp times sin 30°.

steps.prompt: What is the size of the friction force, in newtons?
steps.hint: Friction = μN, and on a ramp the normal force is mg cos 30°, not mg. So 0.20 × 4.0 × 9.8 × cos 30°.

steps.prompt: How much work, in joules, does friction do on the block? Include the sign.
steps.hint: Friction points up the ramp while the block moves down it: W = −6.79 × 5.0.

steps.prompt: What is the block's speed at the bottom, in m/s?
steps.hint: Start energy plus friction's work gives end energy: mgh + W_friction = ½mv². So ½(4.0)v² = 98 − 33.95.

problems.title: Particle on a potential energy curve
problems.prompt: A 1.0 kg particle moves along the x-axis. Its potential energy is U(x) = 2x³ − 6x, in joules, with x in meters. No other forces act on it.

steps.prompt: The last question releases the particle from rest at x = 0 and asks its speed at x = 1 m. Which principle gives that speed straight from U(x), without working out any force's work?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: The work-energy theorem needs the force's work along the path, which the question asks you to avoid; with only this force acting, K + U stays the same.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the force from U(x) is an outside force that speeds the particle up.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the force as a function of time, and you only know U as a function of position.

steps.hint: Only the force from U(x) acts, and it has a potential energy. So the total K + U stays the same as the particle moves.

steps.prompt: How is the force on the particle found from U(x)?
options: F = −dU/dx
F = dU/dx
F = −∫U dx

feedback.F = dU/dx: The sign is wrong: force points toward lower potential energy, so F = −dU/dx.
feedback.F = −∫U dx: This goes the wrong way: U comes from integrating F, so F comes from taking the slope of U.

steps.hint: Force points downhill on the U(x) curve, which is the way U decreases. That is what the minus sign does.

steps.prompt: What is the force on the particle at x = 2.0 m, in newtons? Include the sign.
steps.hint: dU/dx = 6x² − 6, which is 18 at x = 2. Then F = −dU/dx.

steps.prompt: At what positive x, in meters, is the particle in equilibrium (zero force)?
steps.hint: Set dU/dx = 6x² − 6 equal to 0 and keep the positive answer.

steps.prompt: Is the equilibrium at x = 1 m stable or unstable?
options: Stable, because U has a minimum there
Unstable, because U has a maximum there
Neither, because the force is not zero there
steps.answer: Stable, because U has a minimum there

feedback.Unstable, because U has a maximum there: U'' = 12x is positive at x = 1, so U has a minimum there, not a maximum.
feedback.Neither, because the force is not zero t: F = −(6x² − 6) is zero at x = 1, so it is an equilibrium.

steps.hint: The second derivative, 12x, is positive at x = 1, so U curves upward there: a valley. A particle nudged out of a valley is pushed back.

steps.prompt: The particle is released from rest at x = 0 and moves right. What is its speed at x = 1 m, in m/s?
steps.hint: U(0) = 0 and U(1) = −4 J, so 4 J of potential energy became kinetic energy: ½(1.0)v² = 4.

problems.title: Escaping Earth
problems.prompt: Find the speed needed for an object to escape Earth completely (ignore air resistance). Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and its radius is 6.37 × 10⁶ m. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

steps.prompt: Which principle links the launch speed to arriving very far away with no speed left, without working out gravity's work?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: The work-energy theorem needs gravity's work over a huge distance where the force keeps changing, which the question asks you to avoid; K + U stays the same instead.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: Earth's gravity pulls on the object the whole way and slows it.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the force over time, and you don't know how long the trip takes.

steps.hint: Ignoring air, only gravity acts, and gravity has a potential energy. So K + U at launch equals K + U very far away.

steps.prompt: Which formula gives gravitational potential energy when the distance from Earth's center changes a lot?
options: U = −GMm/r
U = mgh
U = GMm/r²

feedback.U = mgh: mgh works only near the surface, where g barely changes.
feedback.U = GMm/r²: GMm/r² is the size of the force, not the energy, and gravitational energy is negative.

steps.hint: mgh only works close to the surface, where g barely changes. GMm/r² is the force, not the energy.

steps.prompt: To just barely escape, what must the object's total energy K + U be at launch?
options: Zero
Negative
Equal to mgR

feedback.Negative: With negative total energy the object stays bound to Earth and falls back.
feedback.Equal to mgR: mgR uses near-surface gravity and is positive; barely escaping means K + U = 0, the same as very far away with no speed left.

steps.hint: Very far away, U is 0, and an object that barely makes it arrives with K = 0. Total energy stays the same, so it was 0 at launch too.

steps.prompt: What is the escape speed, in km/s?
steps.hint: ½mv² − GMm/R = 0 gives v = √(2GM/R). Divide the answer in m/s by 1000.

problems.title: Motor lifting a crate
problems.prompt: A motor and cable lift a 70 kg crate 4.0 m straight up at a steady speed in 5.0 s. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.prompt: The crate's speed doesn't change. Which principle tells you how much work the cable does on the crate?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the cable is an outside force that does work and raises the crate's energy.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: The crate's momentum stays the same only because the cable and gravity balance; it says nothing about work.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: The crate's momentum doesn't change, so its impulse is zero; that can't give the cable's work.

steps.hint: The speed is steady, so the net work is zero: the cable's work plus gravity's work (−mgh) adds up to zero.

steps.prompt: By how much, in joules, does the crate's gravitational potential energy increase?
steps.hint: ΔU = mgΔy = 70 × 9.8 × 4.0. This is also the cable's work.

steps.prompt: What is the motor's average power, in watts?
steps.hint: Average power is work divided by time: 2744 J / 5.0 s.

steps.prompt: With 10 kg more in the crate (80 kg in all), at the same power, how long would the lift take, in seconds?
steps.hint: The work needed is now 80 × 9.8 × 4.0 = 3136 J. Time = work / power = 3136 / 548.8.

problems.title: Car at a steady speed
problems.prompt: A 1200 kg car drives on a level road at 25 m/s. Air resistance and rolling friction together push back on it with 800 N.

steps.prompt: Which principle gives the driving force on the tires from the forces on the car and its acceleration?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
Newton's second law

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the engine keeps adding energy and air resistance keeps removing it.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: The work-energy theorem needs a distance, and none is given; the force comes from the acceleration.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the road and the air push on the car from outside.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs a time and a change in momentum, and neither is given.

steps.hint: You know the car's acceleration (zero at a steady speed, then 0.50 m/s²). The net force equals mass times acceleration.

steps.prompt: At a steady 25 m/s, how big is the driving force from the road on the tires, in newtons?
steps.hint: Steady speed means zero acceleration, so the forward force exactly balances the 800 N pushing back.

steps.prompt: What power, in kilowatts, must the engine deliver?
steps.hint: P = Fv = 800 × 25 watts. Divide by 1000 for kilowatts.

steps.prompt: At the moment the car is at 25 m/s, the driver begins speeding up at 0.50 m/s². What forward force, in newtons, is needed then?
steps.hint: Forward force − 800 = ma = 1200 × 0.50.

steps.prompt: What power, in kilowatts, is the engine delivering at that moment?
steps.hint: P = Fv = 1400 × 25 watts.

problems.title: Bat hits a baseball
problems.prompt: A 0.15 kg baseball moving at 40 m/s is hit straight back at 50 m/s. The bat touches the ball for 1.5 ms (0.0015 s). Take the ball's direction after the hit as positive.

steps.prompt: Which principle links the ball's change in velocity and the 1.5 ms contact time to the bat's average force?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the bat does work on the ball, and energy can't turn a time into a force.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: Work needs how far the bat pushes the ball, and you know the contact time, not the distance.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: The ball's momentum isn't conserved: the bat pushes it from outside, and you know nothing about the bat's motion.

steps.hint: Force times time is impulse, and impulse equals the change in momentum.

steps.prompt: What is the ball's velocity before the hit?
options: 0 m/s

feedback.+40 m/s: Before the hit the ball moved opposite to the positive direction, so its velocity is negative.
feedback.0 m/s: The ball was already moving toward the bat at 40 m/s.

steps.hint: Before the hit the ball moves opposite the positive direction, so its velocity is negative.

steps.prompt: What is the change in the ball's momentum, in kg·m/s?
steps.hint: Δp = m(v_after − v_before) = 0.15 × (50 − (−40)). Subtracting a negative adds.

steps.prompt: What is the average force of the bat on the ball, in newtons?
steps.hint: Impulse = FΔt = Δp, so F = 13.5 / 0.0015.

problems.title: A force that changes with time
problems.prompt: A 2.0 kg object starts at rest. A force F(t) = 12t − 3t² (in newtons, with t in seconds) pushes it in one direction from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s.

steps.prompt: Which principle links the force F(t) over 4.0 s to the object's final speed?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the force is an outside push that adds energy.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: Work needs the force over a distance, and here the force is given as a function of time.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the force is an outside push on the object.

steps.hint: The force is given over time. Adding up F dt gives the impulse, and impulse changes momentum.

steps.prompt: How do you find the impulse from this force?
options: Integrate F(t) dt from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s
Multiply the largest force by 4.0 s
Multiply the force at t = 4.0 s by 4.0 s
steps.answer: Integrate F(t) dt from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s

feedback.Multiply the largest force by 4.0 s: The force is not at its largest the whole time, so this gives too much impulse.
feedback.Multiply the force at t = 4.0 s by 4.0 s: F(4.0) = 0, but the force was not zero the whole time, so this misses the impulse.

steps.hint: The force changes over time, so add up F dt over every small bit of time. That is the area under the F–t graph.

steps.prompt: What is the impulse, in N·s?
What is the object's speed at t = 4.0 s, in m/s?
steps.hint: Impulse = Δp = mv − 0, so v = 32 / 2.0.

problems.title: Car hits a parked truck
problems.prompt: A 1500 kg car moving at 20 m/s hits a parked 2500 kg truck. They lock together and slide as one.

steps.prompt: Which principle gives the speed just after the car and truck lock together, without knowing the force between them?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Kinetic energy isn't kept: crumpling metal turns some of it into heat and sound.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: You would need the work done by the force between them, which you don't know.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: That needs the force between them and how long it lasts, which you don't know.

steps.hint: During the crash the car and truck push only on each other, so their total momentum is the same just before and just after. Vehicles that stick together lose kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: What is their speed just after the collision, in m/s?
steps.hint: Momentum before = 1500 × 20 = 30,000 kg·m/s. After, it is shared by 4000 kg.

steps.prompt: How much kinetic energy is lost in the collision, in kilojoules?
steps.hint: Before: ½ × 1500 × 20² = 300 kJ. After: ½ × 4000 × 7.5² = 112.5 kJ. Subtract.

problems.title: Object breaks into two pieces
problems.prompt: A 3.0 kg object sits at rest, then breaks apart into two pieces. The 1.0 kg piece flies east at 12 m/s. Take east as positive.

steps.prompt: Which principle gives the 2.0 kg piece's velocity without knowing the force of the break?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Kinetic energy isn't kept: the break releases stored energy, so the pieces end with more than they started with.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: You would need the work done by the force of the break, which you don't know.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: That needs the force of the break and how long it lasts, which you don't know.

steps.hint: The pieces push only on each other, so their total momentum stays what it was before the break.

steps.prompt: What is the total momentum of the two pieces just after the break, in kg·m/s?
steps.hint: The pieces only push on each other, so total momentum stays what it was before: the object was at rest.

steps.prompt: What is the velocity of the 2.0 kg piece, in m/s? Include the sign.
What is the velocity of the center of mass of the two pieces after the break, in m/s?
steps.hint: v_cm = total momentum / total mass, and the total momentum is 0.

steps.prompt: How much kinetic energy did the break release, in joules?

problems.title: Elastic head-on collision
problems.prompt: A 2.0 kg ball moving right at 6.0 m/s hits a 4.0 kg ball at rest, head-on. The collision is elastic. Take right as positive.

steps.prompt: Which principle links the two balls' velocities in any collision, elastic or not, without knowing the force between them?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Kinetic energy is kept in this elastic collision, but not in every collision, so it isn't the principle that always holds.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: You would need the work done by the force between the balls, which you don't know.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: That needs the force between the balls and how long it lasts, which you don't know.

steps.hint: The balls push only on each other, so the pair's total momentum is the same before and after, in every collision.

steps.prompt: Which facts together let you solve an elastic collision?
options: Total momentum and total kinetic energy are both conserved
Only total momentum is conserved
Only total kinetic energy is conserved
steps.answer: Total momentum and total kinetic energy are both conserved

feedback.Only total momentum is conserved: In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved too, and two unknown speeds need both facts.
feedback.Only total kinetic energy is conserved: Momentum is conserved in every collision, and two unknown speeds need both facts.

steps.hint: There are two unknown final velocities, so you need two equations. Elastic means kinetic energy is kept as well as momentum.

steps.prompt: What is the 2.0 kg ball's velocity after the collision, in m/s? Include the sign.
steps.hint: For an elastic hit on a ball at rest: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂) × 6.0 = (−2/6) × 6.0. A light ball bounces back off a heavy one.

steps.prompt: What is the 4.0 kg ball's velocity after the collision, in m/s?
Check: what is the total kinetic energy after the collision, in joules?
steps.hint: ½ × 2.0 × 2² + ½ × 4.0 × 4² = 4 + 32. It should equal the 36 J before, because the collision is elastic.

problems.title: Two pucks collide on ice
problems.prompt: A 0.50 kg puck slides east at 4.0 m/s on frictionless ice and hits an identical puck at rest. Afterward, the first puck moves at 2.0 m/s, 60° north of east. Take east as +x and north as +y.

steps.prompt: Which principle gives the second puck's velocity, direction included, without knowing the force between the pucks?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Energy has no direction, so it can't give the second puck's direction; momentum, a vector, can.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: You would need the work done by the force between the pucks, which you don't know, and work has no direction.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: That needs the force between the pucks and how long it lasts, which you don't know.

steps.hint: The ice is frictionless and the pucks push only on each other, so the pair's total momentum, a vector, is the same before and after.

steps.prompt: In a collision in two dimensions, how is momentum conserved?
options: Separately in the x direction and in the y direction
Only along the first puck's starting direction
Only as a total speed, ignoring directions
steps.answer: Separately in the x direction and in the y direction

feedback.Only along the first puck's starting dir: Momentum is a vector, so it is also conserved in the y direction.
feedback.Only as a total speed, ignoring directio: Momentum has a direction, so it is added as a vector, one direction at a time.

steps.hint: Momentum is a vector. Each direction keeps its own total.

steps.prompt: What is the second puck's x-velocity after the collision, in m/s?
steps.hint: The masses are equal, so velocities add up: 4.0 = 2.0 cos 60° + v₂ₓ.

steps.prompt: What is the second puck's y-velocity after the collision, in m/s? Include the sign.
steps.hint: There was no y-momentum before, so 0 = 2.0 sin 60° + v₂ᵧ.

steps.prompt: What is the second puck's speed, in m/s?
steps.hint: Speed = √(vₓ² + vᵧ²) = √(3.0² + 1.73²).

steps.prompt: Was this collision elastic?
options: Yes, the total kinetic energy is the same before and after
No, some kinetic energy was lost
There is no way to tell without the collision time
steps.answer: Yes, the total kinetic energy is the same before and after

feedback.No, some kinetic energy was lost: Work it out: 4.0 J before, and 1.0 J + 3.0 J after, so none was lost.
feedback.There is no way to tell without the coll: Compare kinetic energy before and after; the collision time is not needed.

problems.title: Bullet into a hanging block
problems.prompt: A 0.010 kg bullet is fired into a 2.0 kg wooden block hanging from strings, and stays inside it. The block and bullet swing up, rising 0.20 m. Find the bullet's speed. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.prompt: This has two stages: the bullet hits the block, then the block swings up. Which principle fits the first stage, the bullet stopping inside the block?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Kinetic energy isn't kept during the hit: the bullet tears into the wood and turns much of it into heat.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: You would need the work done by the force between the bullet and the wood, which you don't know.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: That needs the force of the wood on the bullet and how long the hit lasts, which you don't know.

steps.hint: The hit is so quick that the strings and gravity barely change the motion during it. The bullet and block push only on each other, so their total momentum is kept.

steps.prompt: Put the stages of what happens in order.
answer: The bullet hits the block and stops inside it (momentum is conserved)
The block and bullet swing upward together (mechanical energy is conserved)
The block and bullet stop for an instant at the top of the swing
steps.hint: Split the event into the quick collision and the slower swing that follows. Each stage keeps a different quantity.

steps.prompt: Why can't you use energy conservation all the way from the moving bullet to the top of the swing?
options: Kinetic energy is lost when the bullet sticks in the block
Gravity does no work during the swing
The strings do work on the block during the swing
steps.answer: Kinetic energy is lost when the bullet sticks in the block

feedback.Gravity does no work during the swing: Gravity does work as the block rises, and energy conservation allows that; the trouble is the energy lost when the bullet sticks.
feedback.The strings do work on the block during: The strings pull at right angles to the motion, so they do no work.

steps.hint: A collision where things stick is inelastic: most of the bullet's kinetic energy turns into heat and damage to the wood.

steps.prompt: What is the speed of the block and bullet just after the collision, in m/s?
steps.hint: During the swing, energy is conserved: ½v² = gh, so v = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.20).

steps.prompt: What was the bullet's speed before it hit, in m/s?
steps.hint: During the collision, momentum is conserved: 0.010 × v = (0.010 + 2.0) × 1.98.

problems.title: Skaters pull on a rope
problems.prompt: Two skaters stand at rest on frictionless ice, 10 m apart, holding a rope between them. Skater A is 60 kg and skater B is 40 kg. They pull on the rope until they meet.

steps.prompt: Which principle tells you where the skaters meet, using only their masses and starting spots?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Center of mass stays put
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the skaters' muscles add kinetic energy as they pull, and energy doesn't give a meeting point.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: You don't know how hard they pull or how far each one moves, and work gives speeds, not a meeting point.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the pulling force and the time, which you don't know, and it gives momentum, not a position.

steps.hint: The rope's pulls are inside the system. With no outside force, the center of mass keeps its velocity, which is zero here.

steps.prompt: How far from skater A's starting spot do they meet, in meters?
steps.hint: They meet at the center of mass: x_cm = (60 × 0 + 40 × 10) / 100, measured from skater A.

steps.prompt: At one moment skater A moves at 0.80 m/s. How fast is skater B moving then, in m/s?
steps.hint: Total momentum stays zero: 60 × 0.80 = 40 × v_B.

problems.title: Uneven rod snaps on the ice
problems.prompt: A thin rod lies at rest on frictionless ice along the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 2.0 m. It gets heavier toward one end: its mass per meter is λ = 3x kg/m. A small spring catch at x = 1.0 m snaps the rod into two pieces, which slide apart along the x-axis.

steps.prompt: The last question gives the left piece's velocity and asks the right piece's. Which principle links the two, without knowing the catch's force?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved here: the catch releases stored energy you don't know.
feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: You don't know the catch's force or how far it pushes, so you can't find its work.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: That needs the catch's force and how long it pushes, which you don't know.

steps.hint: The catch's push is inside the rod, and the ice is frictionless. So the total momentum stays zero, as it was before the snap.

steps.prompt: What is the rod's total mass, in kg?
steps.hint: M = ∫λ dx = ∫3x dx = 1.5x², from 0 to 2.0.

steps.prompt: Which expression gives the rod's center of mass?
options: x_cm = (∫x λ dx) / M
x_cm = (∫λ dx) / 2.0 m

feedback.x_cm = 2.0 m / 2: The middle is the center of mass only for an even rod, and this one is heavier toward x = 2.0 m.
feedback.x_cm = (∫λ dx) / 2.0 m: ∫λ dx is the mass, so this gives mass per meter, not a position.

steps.hint: Each small piece dm = λ dx counts with weight x. The middle of the rod is only right when the rod is the same all along.

steps.prompt: Where is the center of mass, in meters from x = 0?
steps.hint: ∫3x² dx = x³, which is 8 from 0 to 2.0. Then x_cm = 8 / 6.

steps.prompt: The left piece (x = 0 to 1.0 m) has a mass of 1.5 kg and slides left at 3.0 m/s. What is the right piece's velocity, in m/s? Take +x as positive and include the sign.
steps.hint: Total momentum stays zero. The right piece's mass is 6 − 1.5 = 4.5 kg, so 1.5 × (−3.0) + 4.5 × v = 0.

problems.title: Box sliding to a stop
problems.prompt: A 2.0 kg box slides across a level floor at 4.0 m/s and slows to a stop. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.prompt: Which principle links the box's starting speed to how far it slides before it stops?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: friction turns the box's kinetic energy into heat.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: friction is an outside force that slows the box.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse would give how long the box takes to stop, not how far it slides.

steps.hint: You want a distance. Friction acting over a distance does work, and that work takes away the box's kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: What is the size of the friction force, in newtons?
steps.hint: Friction = μN, and on a level floor N = mg. So 0.25 × 2.0 × 9.8.

steps.prompt: What is the box's starting kinetic energy, in joules?
How far, in meters, does the box slide before it stops?
steps.hint: Friction's work takes away all the kinetic energy: 16 − 4.9 × d = 0, so d = 16 / 4.9.

problems.title: Into a foam bumper
problems.prompt: A {m} kg {thing} moves at v₀ = {v0} m/s along a frictionless track into a foam bumper. The foam crushes and does not spring back. When squeezed a distance x, it pushes back on the {thing} with a force of size βx², where β = {beta} N/m².

steps.prompt: Which principle links the {thing}'s starting speed to how far it squeezes the foam, given the foam's force?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved: the foam crushes and doesn't spring back, so it stores no potential energy.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the bumper is an outside force that stops the {thing}.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the force as a function of time, and here it is given as a function of distance.

steps.hint: The foam's force is given along the path. A force over a distance does work, and that work takes away the {thing}'s kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: Which gives the work the foam does on the {thing} while it is squeezed a distance d?
options: −∫βx² dx from x = 0 to x = d
−βd² × d
−½ × βd² × d
steps.answer: −∫βx² dx from x = 0 to x = d

feedback.−βd² × d: That uses the biggest force, βd², for the whole squeeze, but the force starts at zero and grows.
feedback.−½ × βd² × d: Half the biggest force works only for a force that grows in a straight line, and βx² curves.

steps.hint: The force changes as the foam squeezes, so add up F dx. The work is negative because the foam pushes against the motion.

steps.prompt: What is the {thing}'s kinetic energy just before it reaches the bumper, in joules?
steps.hint: K = ½mv₀² = ½ × {m} × {v0}².

steps.prompt: How much work does the foam do on the {thing} by the time it stops, in joules? Include the sign.
steps.hint: The foam is the only force doing work, and the {thing} stops, so its work equals ΔK = 0 − {K:.2f} J.

steps.prompt: Derive an expression for how far the {thing} squeezes the foam, d, in terms of m, v₀ and β.
steps.hint: −∫βx² dx from 0 to d is −βd³/3. Set it equal to −½mv₀² and solve for d.

steps.prompt: How far does the {thing} squeeze the foam, in meters?
steps.hint: βd³/3 = {K:.2f} J, so d³ = 3 × {K:.2f} / {beta}.

problems.title: Bead sliding on a wire
problems.prompt: A 2.0 kg bead slides without friction along a straight wire on the x-axis. Its potential energy is U(x) = 3x² − 12x, in joules, with x in meters. It is released from rest at x = 0.

steps.prompt: Which principle gives the bead's speed at any point straight from U(x), without working out any force's work?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: The work-energy theorem needs the force's work along the path, which the question asks you to avoid; with no friction, K + U stays the same.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: the force from U(x) is an outside force that speeds the bead up.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the force as a function of time, and you only know U as a function of position.

steps.hint: There is no friction, and the only force along the wire comes from U(x). So the total K + U stays the same as the bead moves.

steps.prompt: What is the force on the bead at x = 0, in newtons? Include the sign.
steps.hint: dU/dx = 6x − 12, which is −12 at x = 0. Then F = −dU/dx.

steps.prompt: At what x, in meters, is the bead in equilibrium (zero force)?
steps.hint: Set dU/dx = 6x − 12 equal to 0.

steps.prompt: What is the bead's speed at x = 2.0 m, in m/s?
steps.hint: U(0) = 0 and U(2) = 12 − 24 = −12 J, so 12 J became kinetic energy: ½(2.0)v² = 12.

steps.prompt: How far to the right, in meters, does the bead go before it turns around?
steps.hint: It turns around where K = 0 again, so U is back to its starting value, 0: 3x² − 12x = 0. Keep the answer that is not x = 0.

problems.title: Probe launched straight up
problems.prompt: A probe leaves Earth's surface moving straight up at 8.0 km/s, with its engine off. Ignore air resistance and Earth's spin. Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and its radius is 6.37 × 10⁶ m. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

steps.prompt: Which principle links the launch speed to the highest point the probe reaches, without working out gravity's work?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: The work-energy theorem needs gravity's work over a large distance where the force keeps changing, which the question asks you to avoid; K + U stays the same instead.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved: Earth's gravity pulls on the probe the whole way up and slows it.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the force over time, and you don't know how long the climb takes.

steps.hint: With the engine off and no air, only gravity acts, and gravity has a potential energy. So K + U at launch equals K + U at the top.

steps.prompt: Does the probe escape Earth or fall back?
options: It falls back, because its total energy K + U is negative
It escapes, because 8.0 km/s is very fast
It escapes, because gravity gets weaker farther away
steps.answer: It falls back, because its total energy K + U is negative

feedback.It escapes, because 8.0 km/s is very fas: Fast isn't enough: escaping needs about 11.2 km/s, the speed that makes K + U zero.
feedback.It escapes, because gravity gets weaker: Gravity gets weaker but never stops; with negative K + U the probe can't get very far away.

steps.hint: Per kilogram, K = ½(8000)² = 3.2 × 10⁷ J and U = −GM/R ≈ −6.25 × 10⁷ J. Their sum is negative, so the probe is bound to Earth.

steps.prompt: How far from Earth's center, in km, is the probe at its highest point?
steps.hint: ½v² − GM/R = −GM/r, with v in m/s. Solve for r, then divide by 1000 for km.

steps.prompt: How high above Earth's surface, in km, does the probe rise?
steps.hint: Subtract Earth's radius, 6370 km, from the distance to the center.

steps.prompt: Using mgh with g = 9.8 m/s² gives a height of only about 3270 km. Why is the real height bigger?
options: Gravity gets weaker with height, so the same energy carries the probe higher
mgh leaves out the probe's mass
mgh measures the height from Earth's center instead of the surface
steps.answer: Gravity gets weaker with height, so the same energy carries the probe higher

feedback.mgh leaves out the probe's mass: The mass cancels in both methods (½mv² = mgh), so it isn't the reason.
feedback.mgh measures the height from Earth's cen: In mgh, h is measured from the surface; the trouble is that g isn't 9.8 m/s² far up.

steps.hint: mgh assumes g stays 9.8 m/s² all the way up. Far from Earth gravity is weaker, so each meter of climb costs less energy.

problems.title: Block down a ramp into another block
problems.prompt: A 1.0 kg block slides from rest down a frictionless curved ramp 0.80 m high. Right at the bottom it hits a 3.0 kg block at rest, and the two stick together. They slide across a rough level floor with a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.40. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.prompt: This has stages. Which principle fits the first stage, the block sliding down the frictionless ramp, without working out any force's work?
options: Conservation of mechanical energy
Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Conservation of momentum
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)

feedback.Work-energy theorem (net work equals cha: The work-energy theorem needs gravity's work along the ramp, which the question asks you to avoid; with no friction, K + U stays the same.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved on the ramp: gravity and the ramp push on the block and change its velocity.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs the forces and how long the slide takes, which you don't know.

steps.hint: On the ramp there is no friction, and only gravity does work. So K + U at the top equals K + U at the bottom.

steps.prompt: Put the stages of what happens in order.
answer: The block slides down the ramp (mechanical energy is conserved)
The blocks hit and stick together (momentum is conserved)
The joined blocks slide to a stop (friction's work takes away their kinetic energy)
steps.hint: Each stage keeps track of something different: energy on the frictionless ramp, momentum in the quick hit, and friction's work on the rough floor.

steps.prompt: What is the block's speed at the bottom of the ramp, in m/s?
What is the speed of the joined blocks just after they stick, in m/s?
steps.hint: Momentum is conserved in the hit: 1.0 × 3.96 = (1.0 + 3.0) × v.

steps.prompt: How far, in centimeters, do the joined blocks slide before they stop?
steps.hint: Friction's work takes away their kinetic energy: 0.40 × 4.0 × 9.8 × d = ½ × 4.0 × 0.99². Then turn meters into centimeters.

lessons.title: 2.1 Systems and Center of Mass
notes: A system is the set of objects you choose to study; forces between them are internal.
Center of mass: x_cm = Σmx / Σm for separate masses, x_cm = (∫x λ dx) / M for a rod.
Internal forces never move the center of mass. With no outside force, it stays put or keeps a steady velocity.

lessons.title: 2.5 Newton's Second Law (with 2.7 Friction)
notes: Net force equals mass times acceleration: ΣF = ma, in each direction separately.
Balanced forces (ΣF = 0) mean constant velocity, including at rest.
Kinetic friction is f = μN, pointing against the sliding.

lessons.title: 3.1 Translational Kinetic Energy
notes: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: K = ½mv².
It is never negative, and doubling the speed makes it four times as big.

lessons.title: 3.2 Work
notes: Constant force: W = Fd cos θ. It is negative when the force points against the motion.
Changing force: W = ∫F dx, the area under the force-position graph.
Work-energy theorem: the net work on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, ΣW = ΔK.

lessons.title: 3.3 Potential Energy
notes: Near Earth, gravitational potential energy changes by ΔU = mgΔy.
A spring stretched or squeezed by x stores U = ½kx².
Force from potential energy: F = −dU/dx. Where U has a minimum, the balance is stable.

lessons.title: 3.4 Conservation of Energy
notes: With only gravity and springs doing work, K + U stays the same.
Friction takes energy out: K₁ + U₁ + W_friction = K₂ + U₂, where W_friction is negative.

lessons.title: 3.5 Power
notes: Power is how fast energy is transferred: P = ΔE/Δt on average.
At an instant, P = Fv for a force along the velocity.

lessons.title: 4.1–4.2 Linear Momentum, Change in Momentum and Impulse
notes: Momentum is p = mv, a vector: its sign shows its direction.
Impulse is J = ∫F dt, the area under a force-time graph, and it equals the change in momentum, Δp.

lessons.title: 4.3 Conservation of Linear Momentum
notes: With no net outside force, a system's total momentum stays the same.
Use it in collisions and explosions: total p before = total p after.

lessons.title: 4.4 Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
notes: Elastic: kinetic energy is also kept. Inelastic: some is lost; when objects stick, the most is lost.
Split a problem into stages: momentum during the quick collision, energy before or after it.

units.title: Unit 6 · Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems

lessons.title: 6.6 Motion of Orbiting Satellites
notes: Far from Earth, gravitational potential energy is U = −GMm/r, zero infinitely far away.
An object escapes if its total energy K + U is zero or more: v_escape = √(2GM/r).
